newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian army general threatened NATO-led force.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian army general threatened NATO-led force.

text.p: A Bosnian army general threatened to use force against NATO-led troops to prevent the confiscation of unauthorised weapons but later backed down, a NATO spokesman said on Monday.

General Atif Dudakovic, Moslem commander of the Bosnian Fifth Corps, issued the threat last week after NATO ordered his troops to hand over anti-aircraft weapons to a storage site, spokesman Major Tony White told reporters.
Fifth Corps soldiers had been seen training with the anti-aircraft missile launchers, which is forbidden under the 1995 Dayton peace treaty, White said.
When troops in NATO's Stabilisation Force (SFOR) arrived to seize the weapons, Dudakovic told a Canadian liaison officer that his men would resist any confiscation.
"The Fifth corps commander said that because he felt that he had not done anything wrong that if anybody attempted to come and take them that they would be engaged," White said.
Dudakovic later withdrew his threat after talks with the British SFOR commander for the northwest region, Major-General Evelyn Webb-Carter.
Dudakovic, regarded as a hero among Moslems for his tough defence of the Bihac enclave during Bosnia's war, "realised he had made a mistake" and agreed to hand over the weapons, according to White.
It was the first time an army officer in Bosnia had issued such a threat against the 31,000-strong NATO-led peace force.
"We don't take the threat lightly at all and that matter is being looked into separately," White said.
The U.S. commander of SFOR, General William Crouch, raised the issue in talks last week with Alija Izetbegovic, the Moslem chairman of the Bosnian collective presidency.
Dudakovic's soldiers assisted NATO in loading the anti-aircraft weapons onto trucks over the weekend. The weapons included two SA-7 anti-aircraft missile launchers and six 30mm anti-aircraft guns.
The Bosnian army was not immediately available for comment.
